mainEntity.name: Why are my teeth sensitive to cold but not hot?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cold sensitivity is often associated with exposed dentine, where the rapid temperature drop causes fluid movement within the microscopic tubules of the tooth, stimulating nerve endings. Hot sensitivity, while also possible, can sometimes indicate a different type of dental issue, such as inflammation of the pulp (pulpitis). If you notice sensitivity primarily to cold, it may suggest early-stage enamel wear or gum recession. However, if you develop sensitivity to heat — particularly if the pain lingers — it is advisable to seek a dental assessment, as this may indicate a condition that benefits from prompt attention.

mainEntity.name: Can sensitive teeth heal on their own?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases, mild sensitivity may improve over time, particularly if it is caused by temporary factors such as recent dental treatment or short-term dietary habits. Using desensitising toothpaste consistently can also help reduce symptoms gradually. However, sensitivity caused by enamel loss, significant gum recession, or tooth damage is unlikely to resolve without some form of intervention. Since enamel does not regenerate once lost, early professional advice can help identify the cause and prevent further progression. Self-management is helpful, but it works best alongside professional guidance.

mainEntity.name: Is tooth sensitivity a sign of a cavity?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tooth sensitivity can sometimes be an early indicator of dental decay, particularly if it is localised to a specific tooth. However, sensitivity has many possible causes, including enamel erosion, gum recession, and bruxism, so it does not automatically mean a cavity is present. The only reliable way to determine whether decay is involved is through a clinical dental examination, which may include X-rays. If your sensitivity is new, persistent, or worsening, a dental check-up can help clarify the cause and provide appropriate guidance.

mainEntity.name: What toothpaste is best for sensitive teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Toothpastes designed for sensitive teeth typically contain active ingredients such as potassium nitrate, which helps calm the nerve inside the tooth, or stannous fluoride, which can help block exposed dentine tubules. Look for products that carry the British Dental Association (BDA) accreditation or similar endorsements. It is important to use desensitising toothpaste regularly — ideally twice daily — as the protective effects build up over time with consistent use. Your dentist can recommend a specific product based on your individual needs and the nature of your sensitivity.

Tooth sensitivity is a commonly reported temporary side effect of teeth whitening procedures. The bleaching agents used in whitening treatments can temporarily increase the permeability of enamel, allowing stimuli to reach the nerve more easily. This sensitivity is usually short-lived and tends to resolve within a few days to a couple of weeks after treatment. If you have pre-existing sensitivity, it is important to discuss this with your dentist before undergoing any whitening treatment, as they can advise on whether the procedure is suitable and suggest ways to minimise discomfort.

mainEntity.name: How often should I visit the dentist if I have sensitive teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you experience ongoing tooth sensitivity, your dentist may recommend more frequent check-ups to monitor the condition and assess whether any underlying cause is progressing. For most patients, a dental examination every six to twelve months is generally recommended, though your dentist will advise on the most appropriate interval based on your individual oral health. Regular visits allow early detection of enamel wear, gum recession, or decay, enabling timely intervention that may prevent sensitivity from worsening.
